title: Cap. III Sol.: two acts of reprobation — praeterition vs praedamnation
pass_a_gloss: Solution. It must be called back to memory what was said in the Prolegomena concerning the twofold act of reprobation; namely, that Reprobation involves these two acts: one negative, which it is permitted to call Passing-by or non-election; the other affirmative, which we can call praedamnation, or Deputing to punishment: I answer therefore, if by reprobation that prior act is understood, although we suppose sin in the reprobated subject, yet we ought not to think that God from the intuition of this sin decreed with himself not to elect or not to free this singular person. For the same sin was also looked upon in those whom he willed to elect and free.
pass_b_english: Sol. Recall what the Prolegomena said of reprobation's twofold act: a negative act — Passing-by or non-election — and an affirmative — praedamnation, or deputing to punishment. If reprobation means that prior act, we may grant sin in the reprobated subject, yet we must not think God from intuition of that sin decreed not to elect or not to free this particular person. He looked on the same sin in those he willed to elect and free.
source_text: Sol. Revocandum est in memoriam, quod de duplici actu reprobationis in Prolegomenis dictum fuit; nimirum, Reprobationem duos hosce actus involvere: unum negativum, quem appellare licet Praeteritionem sive non-electionem; alterum affirmativum, quem vocare possumus praedamnationem, sive Deputationem ad poenam: Respondeo igitur, si per reprobationem prior ille actus intelligatur, quamvis supponamus peccatum in subjecto reprobato, tamen non debemus cogitare Deum ex intuitu peccati hujus decrevisse apud se non eligere aut non liberare hanc personam singularem. Nam idem peccatum in illis etiam intuitus est, quos voluit eligere et liberare.
